messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tax Inspector
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 72

He is 42, a South Asian man who has spent most of his adult life working as a tax inspector, a job he once valued for its order, its rules, and the reassurance that careful attention can prevent costly mistakes. He is married, the father of two school-aged children, and before the event he describes himself as cautious, dependable, “the one who double-checks everything.” That description becomes painful to him now, because the memory that divides his life into before and after is a moment when checking was not enough.

The event happens on an ordinary weekday evening at the end of the financial year, during one of the busiest periods at work. He leaves the office later than planned, mentally preoccupied with disputed filings and a supervisor’s request for revisions by morning. As he drives home through heavy traffic, he keeps replaying numbers in his head, irritated with himself for forgetting to send an email. At an intersection near a market, he turns while the light is changing. He does not see the motorcyclist until impact. Later, he can describe certain details with unbearable clarity—the sound of metal striking metal, the bike sliding, a body on the road, a bag of groceries broken open and rolling into the gutter. He remembers getting out of the car and hearing himself say, over and over, “I’m sorry, I’m sorry,” while other people gather and someone calls for an ambulance. The man survives but sustains severe injuries.

In the first days afterward, he acts as though he can manage by being practical. He gives statements, contacts his insurance company, speaks to police, answers his wife’s worried questions in clipped, factual sentences. But at night, the scene returns in flashes before he can stop it. He sees the rider on the road the moment he closes his eyes. He wakes drenched in sweat, his heart hammering so hard that his wife reaches for him and he jerks away before he knows where he is. He starts sleeping on the edge of the bed, as if ready to spring up. When his children ask why he is tired, he says work is busy.

Driving becomes its own ordeal. At first he takes the long route to avoid the intersection. Then he avoids driving altogether unless absolutely necessary. If he has to get behind the wheel, his shoulders tense before he even starts the engine. He scans every lane, every crossing, every pedestrian with frantic vigilance. A motorcycle passing nearby makes his stomach drop. More than once he pulls over because his hands are shaking too badly to continue. He begins leaving home earlier and taking taxis to the office, telling colleagues that parking has become inconvenient.

At work, the change is visible even though he tries to hide it. Tax inspection requires concentration, judgment, and confidence in one’s decisions. He now reads the same figures repeatedly without absorbing them. He worries that one oversight could destroy someone’s business, just as one moment of inattention destroyed another man’s body. He becomes painfully slow, lingering over minor discrepancies, unable to sign off on files without checking them five or six times. He startles when coworkers approach his desk unexpectedly. The sound of a motorbike from the street below can empty his mind in an instant. Once, during a routine meeting, a colleague mentions a road accident on the news, and he goes silent, staring at the conference table while heat climbs into his face. Later he locks himself in a restroom stall until his breathing settles.

At home he is more distant than angry, though anger appears in sharp, confusing bursts. His wife says he is “here but not here.” He sits with the family but drifts away when conversation turns light or affectionate, as though he no longer deserves ease. He avoids the market near the crash, avoids family outings that require driving, avoids weddings and social gatherings where people might ask ordinary questions about how he has been. He has not told most relatives what happened; the shame feels too large. In private, he imagines what the injured man’s family must think of him. He sometimes looks up news reports or legal updates late at night, then feels sick for days afterward.

What burdens him most is not fear alone but a relentless moral torment. He does not describe the event as bad luck. He describes it as proof that he is dangerous when others trusted him to be careful. He replays tiny decisions from that evening—leaving late, thinking about work, turning when he did—as if, by examining them enough times, he can undo them. When his children run toward the driveway, he shouts too harshly for them to stop, then is flooded with guilt. He no longer cooks over the stove when distracted, no longer climbs a ladder, no longer allows himself small mistakes. His world has narrowed into precaution and punishment.

Months later, he still lives as though the collision is about to happen again or has, in some moral sense, never stopped happening. He moves through his days with a strained, watchful exhaustion. He longs to return to the man he was before that intersection, before the screech and the impact and the sight of another person broken in front of him. But every ordinary act—driving, working, even being with the people he loves—now passes through that moment first.
